turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come in, both of you. Mr Naidoo, your wife asked for this slot — tell me, how's things been at home, in your own words?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm fine, doctor. Truly. I don't even know why we're here. Is this going to take long? I've got the car on a meter.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Shame, he's not fine, doctor. He asks me the same thing three, four times in an hour. Yesterday it was whether the bins go out, over and over.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): I do not. I asked once. You're exaggerating because you're tired. Are you going to write that down?
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm just listening for now. Mrs Naidoo, what else has worried you?
[SEG0006] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He forgot the dentist last Tuesday, and the eye test the week before. I had written both on the calendar. He swears I never told him.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): You never told me. I would have gone. My memory is perfectly alright. How old do you think I am, doctor, ninety?
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): You're seventy-six, it says here. Has he got himself lost at all?

[SEG0009] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ja. Two Saturdays ago he went to Pick n Pay in Plumstead and took the wrong road home, ended up by the robot near the N2. A neighbour saw the bakkie and brought him back. He was gone nearly two hours.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I was not lost. I knew exactly where I was. I just took the scenic way. She panics. Will they take my licence for this?
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nobody is taking anything today. How long have these mix-ups been going on, would you say?
[SEG0012] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Since about last winter. Eight months, easily. Maybe a bit more.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Eight months? Ag, no. If there's anything, it's two or three weeks. After that long weekend. I can't even say the day.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): So we're hearing anything from a few weeks to the better part of a year. We don't have to pin the date down this morning.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Is it Alzheimer's? My neighbour went into a home. Am I going to have to go into a home? Tell me straight.

[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to put a name on it today, and a home is not on the table. Thinking out loud, the things I wouldn't want to miss are a low thyroid, vitamin B12, the tablets, a low mood, or a memory problem itself — but I am not saying any of those is the answer. Let's see what the tests say before anyone concludes anything.
[SEG0017] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He also misplaces his glasses every single morning. That part he might admit.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): The glasses, ja, alright, I do that. They're never where I leave them. But that's just age, isn't it? Everyone does that.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Misplacing glasses happens. I'm more interested in the bigger lapses. Any headaches with all of this?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. I can't tell you when. Is a headache a bad sign? Could it be a tumour?
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): A headache on its own, said like that, I'm not hanging a tumour on it. Any falls, or chest pain, or feeling short of breath?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No falls. No chest pain. Breathing is fine. Why, what are you looking for?
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Just making sure nothing acute is hiding. How's your sleep?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Sometimes, not really. I mean I sleep. Mostly. Don't write that I don't sleep.
[SEG0025] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He is up at three worrying, most nights. He asks me if the door is locked, then asks again.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): That is not most nights. Don't say most nights.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Waterworks, bowels, any change there?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): All fine. Normal. Is this relevant?
[SEG0029] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Doctor, I should say, I do the medicines. He doesn't fill his own pill box. I pack it Sunday nights.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's helpful. What is he actually on?
[SEG0031] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Perindopril in the morning for the blood pressure, and simvastatin 20 milligrams at night for the cholesterol. He's been on both for years.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): The blood pressure one is 8 milligrams. She always says 4. I know my own tablets. Don't I?
[SEG0033] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's 4 milligrams, doctor. The packet says 4. He gets mixed up with the old dose from before they reduced it.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll leave the dose blank in my mind until I see the packet. Anything else in the box?

[SEG0035] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): A small white tablet at bedtime for sleep — I can never remember the name, looks a bit like a tiny oval. Maybe half, I'm not a hundred percent on the dose. Not every night, perhaps three times a week when he's restless.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): I take it every night. She forgets to give it and then says I don't need it. Are you going to stop it? I won't sleep at all if you stop it.

[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): I was going to say we should stop that sleeping tablet, given the muddle. But if it's only some nights and we don't even have the name straight, I'll leave it for now. Bring the box next visit and we'll decide then. Don't change anything yourself.
[SEG0038] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He used to take a Disprin every day. The day hospital sister stopped that, oh, last year. He's not on it now.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. And how sure are we the perindopril and the statin actually get taken?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. I take them. I think.
[SEG0041] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): If I pack the box, they go. When I'm at my sister in Hermanus for a weekend, I'm not sure. Last month I came back and Thursday and Friday were still in the box.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines or anything else?
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing. I'm not allergic to a thing.
[SEG0044] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): That's not quite right. Years ago, penicillin gave him a rash, and the clinic said avoid it. We've avoided it since.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): That was my brother, not me. I told you. I have no allergy. Will penicillin come up in the blood test?
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): The blood test won't test for that. I'll note that the two of you don't agree, and we won't give penicillin unless it's clarified. Any family memory problems?
[SEG0047] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His mother had Alzheimer's, late on. She died at eighty-nine.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): She was just old. But ja, they called it that. Does that mean I'll get it? Be honest.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): It raises the background a bit, it doesn't decide your case. Any recent blood tests you remember the clinic mentioning?

[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, last year at the day hospital they did a sugar test and they said it was borderline. Not diabetes, they said. Borderline. Should I be on a tablet for that? What was the number? I never got the number.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): We won't treat a number nobody can remember. I'll repeat the sugar with the other bloods. Do you smoke, or take a drink?

[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Never smoked, and just a glass of red with the braai on a Saturday. We live together, just the two of us, in the house in Diep River, and I retired from the post office, what, ten years back. Is retirement bad for the brain?
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, and the load shedding last night killed the alarm, that's why we were late, not because I forgot. The robot on Main was out as well.

[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): These things happen. Let me just check you over — blood pressure is one thirty-eight over eighty-four, pulse seventy-two, heart sounds are normal, and there's no weakness in the arms or the legs.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): Is one thirty-eight high? Should I go to hospital? How long will I sit here?

[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): One thirty-eight over eighty-four is acceptable on that tablet. No hospital today. At first I thought a CT scan of the head, and I'd see you again in six months if the bloods were alright.
[SEG0057] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He got properly lost in the bakkie, doctor. And he's anxious enough without a scan. Also that borderline sugar — nobody followed it up.

[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fair, scratch the CT — I'm not ordering a scan today. What I will do is bloods: thyroid, B12, sugar, kidneys, and a full blood count, and I'll refer you for a memory assessment. I'll see you back here in three weeks, not six months, with whatever results we have.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): A memory assessment? What do they do? Is it a pass or fail? Will they tell the traffic department? How many tubes of blood? Does it hurt?

[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's a proper look at memory, not a driving test, and I won't be phoning the traffic department off this visit. A few tubes, a small scratch, results usually within the week. Please don't drive until we've had that assessment — let your wife take the bakkie.
[SEG0061] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll drive. And I'll keep packing the pill box, and I'll bring the packets when we come back.
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): So you're not saying I've got dementia. Say it again. And if the memory place has a long waiting list, what then? Do I just sit?

[SEG0063] person_1 (DOCTOR): I am not saying dementia. I am not saying anything firm until the tests speak. If the memory assessment can't see you within the month, phone the rooms and we'll bring the three-week visit forward. Any other question before I let you go?
[SEG0064] person_2 (PATIENT): Just — if I feel worse, like more confused, do I come back sooner? And is it alright to have the braai on Saturday, a glass of wine?
[SEG0065] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes, come back sooner if the confusion is clearly worse, or if there's a fall or weakness. One glass with the braai is fine. We'll stop there.
[SEG0066] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Come, we'll sort the parking meter. Thank you, doctor.

The patient only supposed he sometimes has a headache and said not really, and he cannot say when it began.
The spouse says perindopril is 4 mg and the patient says it is 8 mg.
The spouse said the unnamed sleeping tablet is maybe half a tablet and is not a hundred percent sure of the dose.
The spouse cannot name the small white oval tablet used for sleep.

The patient denies any allergy and says the penicillin rash was his brother's, while the spouse recalls that years ago penicillin gave him a rash, the clinic said to avoid it, and it has been avoided since.

spec.situation: Spouse brings an older person who 'is fine' but repeats questions, forgets appointments and got lost; patient disagrees on many points; medicines managed by spouse; doctor plans bloods and a memory assessment, no diagnosis said aloud.
features: ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.

doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.
test_result_recalled: the patient reports an old test or result ('they said it was borderline'); recorded as reported history/investigation only as far as said, not as a confirmed value.

bad.reason: Sleeping tablet current for sleep supported; 'half tablet' is uncertain, not established.
bad.text: Small white oval sleeping tablet (dose=half tablet, indication=sleep, status=currently_used, reported_by=family_member)

bad.reason: Doctor said bring the box next visit; extracted fact says medication box.
bad.text: Bring the medication box next visit (action_type=other, status=recommended, responsible_person=patient)

omissions.text: Sleeping tablet use is disputed: spouse said it is taken not every night, perhaps three times a week when he is restless, but the patient said he takes it every night.
Doctor initially said they should stop the sleeping tablet because of the muddle, but then decided to leave it unchanged for now until the medication box/packets are brought next visit.

Medication adherence detail missing: when wife was away for a weekend, Thursday and Friday doses were still in the pill box, raising concern that perindopril/statin may be missed if she does not pack/supervise.
Denied finding on review of systems not recorded: patient said breathing is fine / no shortness of breath.
Headache symptom was very uncertain/minimal: patient said 'Sometimes, not really' and could not say when, rather than a clear current headache.
Past history/investigation detail missing: prior blood sugar at the day hospital last year was described as 'borderline', specifically 'not diabetes' per patient, and no number was available.

Doctor documented differential considerations that could explain the memory problem: low thyroid, vitamin B12 deficiency, medication effects, low mood, or a memory problem itself, without diagnosing any of them.

Plan change/disagreement not captured: doctor first considered CT head and follow-up in six months if bloods were alright, then after discussion decided not to order CT and instead review in three weeks.
Doctor advised that memory assessment is not a driving test and said he would not be phoning the traffic department off this visit.
If the memory assessment cannot see him within the month, the doctor said to phone the rooms and they would bring the three-week visit forward.
